item.title: The Shokz OpenRun Pro open-ear sport headphones drop to $100 at Best Buy
item.itunes:title: The Shokz OpenRun Pro open-ear sport headphones drop to $100 at Best Buy
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you run or work out outdoors, earbuds that seal off your ears can make it harder to hear traffic, cyclists, or someone calling your name. Open-ear headphones avoid that by leaving your ears uncovered, and that's the idea behind the Shokz OpenRun Pro. Right now, you can get them for $99.99 at Best Buy, $60 off the normal price.

Bone conduction makes the OpenRun Pro our choice for outdoor runners. The open-ear design won't occlude your ear canal, so you can still listen to music while remaining aware of what's going on around you. Available in four colors and two band sizes, the OpenRun Pro fit gently yet securely around the back of the head, looping around the ears and resting against the temples. This pair is equipped with Bluetooth 5.0 and feature PremiumPitch 2.0+, which prevents bleed and minimizes distortion.

$99 at Best Buy

What makes the Shokz OpenRun Pro headphones so good?

Open-ear audio built for workouts

Credit: Shokz

Essentially, Shokz's open-ear headphones are created specifically with athletes in mind. Since your ears are uncovered, you can hear your surroundings, which is safer than noise-canceling alternatives, especially when you're out running.

You also get about 10 hours of playback per charge, which is plenty for long training sessions, and a 5-minute charge gives you roughly 90 minutes of listening. For calls, there are dual noise-canceling microphones. The companion app adds Standard and Vocal EQ modes, so you can adjust the sound to taste.

There are trade-offs, however. The IP55 rating covers rain and sweat but not water sports. Bluetooth is limited to the SBC codec, the magnetic charging port on the back needs Shokz's proprietary cable, and the bass trails what you'd get from in-ear headphones. So the OpenRun Pros make the most sense if you run or train outdoors and want to keep an ear on your surroundings. If you mostly listen to bass-heavy music, or you want headphones for water sports, you'd be better off looking elsewhere.

If you want open-ear headphones for running or the gym and can live with the trade-offs, we think $99.99 is a fair price for the OpenRun Pro. Just be sure to grab them from Best Buy while the holiday deal is still on.

item.title: This file manager lives entirely in a terminal window, and it’s better than your GUI
item.itunes:title: This file manager lives entirely in a terminal window, and it’s better than your GUI
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Plenty of Linux users who live in a terminal still have a GUI file manager, and they reach for it when it's time to shuffle files around. There's nothing wrong with that, and a terminal can do the job just as well, but terminal file managers have a reputation for either looking or feeling decades-old to use.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

superfile doesn't fall into either of those categories, and it's the first terminal file manager I've used that I would reach for over a GUI. It's launched with a single command and is designed to look and behave a lot like a graphical interface you already know. It definitely doesn't make GUIs redundant for file management, but it can go places they can't, and I find myself opening it more than my old default.

6 free file managers on Linux that are better than anything on Windows

They're just that good!

22
By  Ayush Pande

Getting started with superfile is easy

It's laid out a lot like the file manager you're familiar with already

superfile is packaged almost everywhere Linux users get software. On Arch and its derivatives, it’s a single pacman install, and there’s also Homebrew, a Nix package, and a one-line install script. Launch it with spf, and run spf pl to print the paths to its config and hotkey files. Vim users will be happy to know that there's a vim-style hotkey file you can swap to that's included in the project.

The layout looks and feels pretty natural by default. The main file panel sits next to a sidebar of pinned folders and mounted drives, which does the same job as the Places list in Files or Dolphin. Below are panels for metadata, the clipboard, and running processes. The processes panel tracks copies and moves the way a GUI progress indicator does, and having all of this on one window is very refreshing.

The shortcuts feel familiar too. Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, and Ctrl+V all perform copy, cut, and paste duties respectively. Ctrl+N creates a new file, or a folder if the name ends in a slash, and Ctrl+R renames. Ctrl+D sends the selection to the trash, which is the same trash your desktop uses.

Like most GUI file managers, you can open multiple panels in superfile, and you can move across them using Tab, and that can make moving or copying files so much less tedious. You can open as many panels as your monitor allows compared to Dolphin's two and GNOME Files' zero, so that's already a marked improvement.

For bulk work, v switches to select mode, where Shift and the arrow keys sweep up a run of files and Shift+A grabs the whole directory. From there you can copy, cut, or trash the lot, or compress it with Ctrl+A. Ctrl+E does the opposite, and will extract archives. It also has more than 20 built-in themes, which should cover virtually all of your bases in terms of how you want it to look.

This free self-hosted file explorer links all of my storage into one web-based UI

I set up a self-hosted file manager that lets me browse local drives, cloud storage, and network shares, all from one clean web interface.

By  Pranav Bhardwaj

Previews and metadata without touching a mouse

My favorite feature

The preview pane is on by default, but you can toggle it using f. In this pane, text files, folders, and images all render inside it, and while it might sound small, this is by far my favorite feature of superfile. superfile produces sharp image previews in terminals that support it, and that's huge for browsing through large batches of images, which is something I do in my daily workflow. These previews also load asynchronously, so scroling past big swaths of large image files doesn't stall the interface.

Pressing m focuses the metadata panel, which shows things like permissions, owner, group, and so on. Folder sizes only render while the panel is focused, so you're not sizing up every directory you scroll past. There's a lot more you're able to do in this panel, like view Linux file attributes and show EXIF data through a plugin, but even at default it's a valuable feature.

6 free file managers on Linux that are better than anything on Windows

They're just that good!

22
By  Ayush Pande

The tricks your desktop file manager can't pull off

superfile has a deep bag

For those who have been in GUIs most of their computing lives, living in a terminal might seem like a limitation, but it's a feature here. With zoxide installed and support enabled, pressing z opens a jump panel for your most used directories. If you also turn on cd_on_quit and add the short wrapper from the docs, quitting superfile with q will now leave you in whatever directory you were just browsing. That turns it from something you use to look at files into something you use to actually get around your file system.

When you land on a file you want to edit, pressing e will open that file in the default editor, and Shift+E opens the whole directory. You can map which programs you want to open specific file types in the config as well, so it's not always using the system default.

Perhaps the biggest bonus of superfile is its ability to run anywhere a terminal will, and that means it works pretty much flawlessly over SSH. I can SSH into my Proxmox server and, as long as superfile is installed, I can run it and use all the same keybinds and panels as I do on the desktop. It makes it super easy to quickly parse through configuration files and make quick changes without needing to cd through directories constantly. A super valuable addition for anyone running a home lab with a large selection of services like myself.

Another thing that surprised me about superfile is its compatibility—I initially discovered it as a Linux tool, but you can install and use it on Windows and even macOS, too.

I switched to the COSMIC Linux desktop, and I can't wait for the future

COSMIC is out of this world, even with its flaws

15
By  João Carrasqueira

A GUI still earns its keep for some things, but superfile is invaluable on all of my Linux installs

superfile is great, but you can't drag files from a superfile window to another app, or open network drives that aren't mounted, and those are the things I still use a GUI for. But that's the thing, you don't have to uninstall your GUI file manager to use superfile. It can live right alongside whatever you currently use, and you can even launch it straight from an app launcher like you would something like Dolphin. It's just another tool in the toolbox for Linux users, and it's one that I'll be installing on all of my machines going forward.

item.title: Upgrade your PC's wireless speeds for just $30 with this ASUS Wi-Fi 6 adapter
item.itunes:title: Upgrade your PC's wireless speeds for just $30 with this ASUS Wi-Fi 6 adapter
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If your desktop has no Wi-Fi, or your laptop's wireless card is showing its age, a USB adapter is the easiest way to get onto Wi-Fi 6 without opening the case. Thankfully, you can pick up something like the ASUS Dual Band Wi-Fi 6 USB Adapter. Right now, you can grab this helpful gadget from Amazon for just $29.99, 40% off its regular $49.99 price.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
ASUS USB-AX55 Nano
Brand
ASUS
Wi-Fi Standard
Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax), AX1800
Max speeds
1,800Mbps (1,201Mbps 5GHz, 574Mbps 2.4GHz)
Dimensions
1 × 0.63 × 0.35 in (25.5 × 16 × 9 mm)
Weight
0.14 oz (4g)
Color
Black

The ASUS USB-AX55 Nano is a compact AX1800 dual-band WiFi 6 USB adapter for desktops and laptops. It supports 160MHz channels, 1024-QAM, OFDMA and MU-MIMO, and WPA3 security, with up to 1201Mbps on 5GHz and 574Mbps on 2.4GHz.

See at Amazon

A simple way to boost your wireless speeds

The main draw here is, of course, Wi-Fi 6 capabilities. You're looking at speeds up to 1201 Mbps on the 5GHz band and up to 574 Mbps on the 2.4GHz band. ASUS claims it's up to 1.5X faster than a Wi-Fi 5 client, though that figure is based on the company's specific test conditions (5GHz, 80MHz channels). It's also backward compatible with Wi-Fi 5 and older standards, so it'll still connect to a router that hasn't been upgraded—you just won't get the full effects of Wi-Fi 6, including access to OFDMA and MU-MIMO features.

The adapter also lives up to its 'Nano' moniker, measuring just 1.0 x 0.63 x 0.35 inches and weighing 0.16 ounces. It's small enough that it's easy to leave attached even to a laptop. Keep in mind that ASUS lists support only for 64-bit Windows 11 and Windows 10. It isn't listed for macOS, Chromebooks, or Linux, so check your operating system before picking up this adapter.

Used Wi-Fi 6 routers are still a better home networking deal than Wi-Fi 7 routers for most homes

You can boost coverage and performance for a fraction of the cost

4
By  Tanveer Singh

If you're on Windows and want Wi-Fi 6 without opening your PC, $29.99 at Amazon is an easy price to like. Just be sure to grab it while it's still on sale.

item.itunes:title: My PS5 Pro and TV are ready for GTA 6, and the tweaks took less than 10 minutes
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
We're in the endgame now — Grand Theft Auto 6 is just days away, and my PlayStation 5 Pro has pre-downloaded over 200GB of the GTA 6 Ultimate Edition. Unless you've been living under a rock, the internet right now is full of people frantically buying VRR-friendly TVs and PS5 Pro consoles to best enjoy GTA 6.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Among the millions of day-one players, though, you'd be surprised by how many have fantastic TVs and consoles but won't get the best possible experience — they never took the time to optimize both their consoles and displays.

And with the game's preload now available, there's even more reason to do it. Whether you're on a PS5 Pro or want your console and TV working their best, a handful of settings are worth checking right now. Some take seconds to change, others are buried in menus, but none require you to be a home-theater nerd.

Get your PS5 talking to your TV properly

You can't optimize what the console isn't outputting

Before touching a single picture setting on the TV, make sure your console is actually sending it everything your display can handle. Head into Settings > Screen and Video, and you'll see multiple settings best left on Automatic — Resolution, 120Hz Output, HDR, VRR, ALLM, Deep Color Output, and RGB Range. This lets the console negotiate the appropriate signal instead of forcing settings that may create more problems than they solve.

The 120 Hz Output option here is particularly important, folks. Even a base PS5 has this option, so it's best to keep it turned on or set to Automatic. Regardless of whether a game gets near 120fps, a 120Hz signal gives compatible games access to high-refresh modes while also enabling 40fps modes.

On a regular 60Hz display, 40 FPS modes result in horrible frame-pacing compromises, since only a 120Hz panel divides cleanly into a 40 FPS output, keeping each frame onscreen for three refreshes. Leave VRR enabled, too; the PlayStation 5 (and Pro) will use it when a game supports it, and you don't gain anything by manually babysitting the setting.

Lastly, check the actual physical connection between the TV and the PlayStation. Your console should be connected directly to a full-bandwidth HDMI 2.1 port on your TV. Some TVs have only one or two ports capable of 4K at 120Hz, so plugging the console into the wrong socket can turn your expensive setup into a very expensive 60Hz machine. Oh, and all this only works if you're using an Ultra High Speed HDMI cable.

5 components that make my life easier as a PC and PS5 gamer

I won't be able to live without them today.

3
By  Samarveer Singh

Stop your TV from fighting your PS5 Pro

Your TV has no business "helping" you this much

Once you've configured your console properly, it's time to stop the TV from undoing all that work. Start by enabling Game Mode or the equivalent of that feature on your TV. Samsung, LG, Sony, Hisense, and TCL all call it something slightly different, but the goal is the same— it cuts out unnecessary processing and keeps input latency as low as possible. If your TV supports Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM), then your PS5, PS5 Pro, or Xbox Series X/S will automatically switch into this mode.

Next, turn off the stuff that exists primarily to make television broadcasts look less terrible. TVs love forcibly turning on settings like motion smoothing, noise reduction, MPEG noise reduction, artificial sharpness, dynamic contrast, and AI picture enhancements, which can introduce processing games don't need.

I'd also disable the TV's Eco Mode, Energy Saving, and ambient-light compensation features. These dynamically alter the TV's brightness, which is particularly irritating in HDR games where you want explosions, headlights, and neon signs in Leonida to look consistent and attractive.

However, if you have a mini-LED, QLED, or LCD TV (anything with a backlight, really), make sure you never turn off Local Dimming. It's imperative to keep it enabled and generally set it to High. If it gets too dark, try tweaking the settings to find the right spot without making the picture too washed out or too bright. Local dimming, after all, is one of the reasons you bought the expensive TV in the first place. On an OLED, though, there's no backlight, so there are no local-dimming zones to babysit.

GTA 6 data-mining has revealed some interesting details

Even the PS5 Pro isn't getting a higher-FPS mode

The GTA 6 preload went live on November 10, and data miners have already picked it apart, pored over it, and analyzed it a thousand different ways. Even though Rockstar has confirmed a 30 FPS target framerate for GTA 6, files found in the PS5 build point to a 120Hz High framerate mode.

No, this doesn't mean what one might think — GTA 6 will not run at 120 FPS. 120Hz is just the display refresh rate, and not the game's own rendering rate. For now, I'd make sure 120Hz Output is enabled on the PlayStation 5, the PS5 Pro, and your Xbox Series X/S console, if you have one. This will ensure that you're ready for whatever Rockstar actually ships.

The 120Hz Output support is a very interesting new addition to GTA 6-related news. A 120Hz display can show a perfectly paced 40 FPS signal, with each frame displayed for three refreshes. That gives you a 25ms frame time instead of the 33.3ms of 30 FPS, without demanding anywhere near the rendering power required for 60 FPS. Sadly, Rockstar has confirmed that GTA 6 will be locked to 30 FPS even on a PlayStation 5 Pro. Regardless, it's always worth keeping 120Hz Output enabled on your console.

The preload reportedly doesn't point to VRR support either, but I'd still leave VRR enabled on the PS5 Pro. It remains useful in your other games, and there's no reason to keep toggling it manually. If GTA 6 doesn't use it, the console simply won't engage VRR for that game.

The useful part is having the display ready for whatever high-refresh mode Rockstar has prepared — and not discovering on launch day that your $2,000 television has been sitting at 60Hz the entire time.

The PlayStation 5 Pro still has some tricks up its sleeve, though

GTA 6 isn't chasing 60 FPS, but the Pro isn't just pushing pixels

The preload data also points to a newer PSSR implementation, with a version value of 13.60 compared with the 13.00-series version seen in existing PS5 Pro games. We don't yet know how much better it is, but Rockstar has now confirmed that PS5 Pro gets improved clarity through PSSR. There is also a High CPU Frequency Mode flag in the files, which suggests that Rockstar will be squeezing out all the additional CPU performance from the Pro.

The more interesting Pro-exclusive discovery is additional ray-tracing data, which lines up rather nicely with Rockstar's official confirmation of ray-traced shadows exclusive to PS5 Pro. With GTA 6 targeting 30 FPS on both the PlayStation 5 and PS5 Pro, the Pro's job is therefore to make those 30 frames look better instead of magically manufacturing another 30 of them.

There are also early references to multiplayer activity and session-launch functions buried in the PS5 data, hinting that GTA Online is lurking somewhere behind the curtain. That's not something Rockstar has officially detailed yet, so I'm not changing any settings around it.

For now, though, the to-do list is rather simple — configure your display for the best possible 30 FPS experience, because that's what Rockstar is promising. Let the Pro spend its extra hardware making those frames count.

Before GTA 6 comes out, I'm playing the entirety of GTA 5 completely in my web browser

Ctrl+T for Los Santos.

By  Samarveer Singh

Ten minutes now is better than regret on launch day

It would be ridiculous to spend a small fortune on a PS5 Pro and a gorgeous television, only to leave both running on their default settings and never question whether you're actually getting what you paid for. I've done enough tinkering with displays to know the difference between a good setup and a great one often comes down to knowing where the darn switches are.

Give yourself ten minutes, make the changes once, and forget about them. When Rockstar finally drops us into Leonida, I'd much rather worry about which car to steal first than wonder why my TV looks weird.

item.title: My Ethernet connection was running at a fraction of its rated speed, and the problem wasn't my router
item.itunes:title: My Ethernet connection was running at a fraction of its rated speed, and the problem wasn't my router
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Whenever I'm having trouble with my internet connection, especially speed- or latency-related issues, the first thing I usually do is restart my router. If that doesn't work, I'm quick to blame its aging hardware or complain to my ISP because what else could realistically be the problem? So when I noticed my Steam downloads struggling to break 100Mbps despite having a 500Mbps fiber connection, I started wondering whether it was time to ditch the D-Link DIR-882 that I've had for eight years.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Except this time, the problem had nothing to do with my router or ISP. I was still getting the speeds I paid for on my iPhone and MacBook over Wi-Fi, so I knew the issue was specific to my wired connection. Even though I hadn't changed any network settings recently, I still suspected something was wrong with my PC. The confusing bit was that my Ethernet connection was otherwise stable, with no random disconnects. But then I checked the link speed in Windows, and that's when things started making sense.

Don't blame your router for slow speeds until you've tested your Ethernet cables

The physical layer is often at fault

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

The link speed narrowed down the problem

Windows was reporting 100Mbps instead of 1Gbps

Let me walk you through my thought process while troubleshooting this. Since I was getting close to 500Mbps as per my plan over Wi-Fi, I was pretty sure my ISP wasn't responsible this time. But that didn't rule out my router because I knew a faulty LAN port could still affect my wired connection. That's what pushed me to go to Settings -> Network & internet -> Ethernet and check the Aggregated link speed, where I found Windows reporting 100Mbps instead of 1000Mbps. For context, this is the maximum negotiated connection rate between my PC and router over Ethernet, not my actual internet speed.

At this point, I still wasn't sure what exactly was limiting the link speed because I knew my D-Link DIR-882 has Gigabit LAN ports and the cable was plugged into the 5GbE port on my X870E motherboard. And I clearly remembered using a Cat6 cable, which should have no trouble handling a Gigabit connection. At first, I tried different ports on both my router and motherboard, but that didn't change anything. That left the cable as my next suspect. So I grabbed a spare Cat6 cable, plugged it in, and checked the link speed again. Sure enough, Windows reported 1000Mbps, as it should.

A faulty cable doesn't have to stop working

It can still establish a connection, just at a lower speed

Now you might be wondering, wouldn't a damaged cable just stop working completely? Not quite. You see, a standard copper Ethernet cable has eight wires arranged into four twisted pairs. Gigabit Ethernet over twisted-pair copper, also called 1000BASE-T, needs all four pairs to work properly. But Fast Ethernet (100BASE-TX), which operates at 100Mbps, only needs two of those pairs. So if one of the wires or contacts needed for Gigabit Ethernet is damaged, the connection can fall back to 100Mbps instead of dropping entirely.

This is why it took me multiple other troubleshooting steps before I started suspecting the cable. As far as I was concerned, if the cable was faulty, I'd either have no internet connection or experience random disconnects. So, how did I damage mine, you ask? I don't know for sure because I didn't see any obvious physical damage, but repeated bending is enough to damage the copper wires inside. A bad crimp or a loose contact inside the connector can also affect the connection, even if the cable looks fine from the outside.

But don't assume your cable's at fault

It's still the easiest thing to replace, though

In my case, replacing the Ethernet cable fixed the problem, but that doesn't mean yours is necessarily faulty if Windows shows a 100Mbps link speed. As I said earlier, a damaged LAN port on your router or motherboard can also lead to this exact issue. Apart from that, I also recommend checking your network adapter's Speed & Duplex setting in Device Manager. You'll find it under Property in the Advanced tab. If this is manually set to 100Mbps Full Duplex instead of Auto Negotiation, that could be your answer.

That said, I still don't think replacing the Ethernet cable is a bad place to start, especially once you've ruled out your settings. There's a good chance you already have a spare lying around, and even if you don't, you can get a 25-foot cable for under $10. Sure, if you have a second LAN port on your motherboard as I do, you can try that first, but not everyone has that luxury. And spending money on a new router is probably the last thing you'd want to do, anyway.

My router gets to live another day

Considering I've been using this router since 2018, I was almost convinced it was finally time to upgrade when I ran into this issue. With all these Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 7 routers available today, it's really hard not to. But all I really needed was a different cable, and I already had a spare in the drawer. For now, my router handles my 500Mbps fiber connection just fine, so until I actually hit its limits, I don't see a reason to replace it. Maybe that'll change when I eventually upgrade to a Gigabit plan.

Whenever I'm having trouble with my internet connection, especially speed- or latency-related issues, the first thing I usually do is restart my router. If that doesn't work, I'm quick to blame its aging hardware or complain to my ISP because what else could realistically be the problem? So when I noticed my Steam downloads struggling to break 100Mbps despite having a 500Mbps fiber connection, I started wondering whether it was time to ditch the D-Link DIR-882 that I've had for eight years.

Except this time, the problem had nothing to do with my router or ISP. I was still getting the speeds I paid for on my iPhone and MacBook over Wi-Fi, so I knew the issue was specific to my wired connection. Even though I hadn't changed any network settings recently, I still suspected something was wrong with my PC. The confusing bit was that my Ethernet connection was otherwise stable, with no random disconnects. But then I checked the link speed in Windows, and that's when things started making sense.

Don't blame your router for slow speeds until you've tested your Ethernet cables

The physical layer is often at fault

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

The link speed narrowed down the problem

Windows was reporting 100Mbps instead of 1Gbps

Let me walk you through my thought process while troubleshooting this. Since I was getting close to 500Mbps as per my plan over Wi-Fi, I was pretty sure my ISP wasn't responsible this time. But that didn't rule out my router because I knew a faulty LAN port could still affect my wired connection. That's what pushed me to go to Settings -> Network & internet -> Ethernet and check the Aggregated link speed, where I found Windows reporting 100Mbps instead of 1000Mbps. For context, this is the maximum negotiated connection rate between my PC and router over Ethernet, not my actual internet speed.

At this point, I still wasn't sure what exactly was limiting the link speed because I knew my D-Link DIR-882 has Gigabit LAN ports and the cable was plugged into the 5GbE port on my X870E motherboard. And I clearly remembered using a Cat6 cable, which should have no trouble handling a Gigabit connection. At first, I tried different ports on both my router and motherboard, but that didn't change anything. That left the cable as my next suspect. So I grabbed a spare Cat6 cable, plugged it in, and checked the link speed again. Sure enough, Windows reported 1000Mbps, as it should.

A faulty cable doesn't have to stop working

It can still establish a connection, just at a lower speed

Now you might be wondering, wouldn't a damaged cable just stop working completely? Not quite. You see, a standard copper Ethernet cable has eight wires arranged into four twisted pairs. Gigabit Ethernet over twisted-pair copper, also called 1000BASE-T, needs all four pairs to work properly. But Fast Ethernet (100BASE-TX), which operates at 100Mbps, only needs two of those pairs. So if one of the wires or contacts needed for Gigabit Ethernet is damaged, the connection can fall back to 100Mbps instead of dropping entirely.

This is why it took me multiple other troubleshooting steps before I started suspecting the cable. As far as I was concerned, if the cable was faulty, I'd either have no internet connection or experience random disconnects. So, how did I damage mine, you ask? I don't know for sure because I didn't see any obvious physical damage, but repeated bending is enough to damage the copper wires inside. A bad crimp or a loose contact inside the connector can also affect the connection, even if the cable looks fine from the outside.

But don't assume your cable's at fault

It's still the easiest thing to replace, though

In my case, replacing the Ethernet cable fixed the problem, but that doesn't mean yours is necessarily faulty if Windows shows a 100Mbps link speed. As I said earlier, a damaged LAN port on your router or motherboard can also lead to this exact issue. Apart from that, I also recommend checking your network adapter's Speed & Duplex setting in Device Manager. You'll find it under Property in the Advanced tab. If this is manually set to 100Mbps Full Duplex instead of Auto Negotiation, that could be your answer.

That said, I still don't think replacing the Ethernet cable is a bad place to start, especially once you've ruled out your settings. There's a good chance you already have a spare lying around, and even if you don't, you can get a 25-foot cable for under $10. Sure, if you have a second LAN port on your motherboard as I do, you can try that first, but not everyone has that luxury. And spending money on a new router is probably the last thing you'd want to do, anyway.

My router gets to live another day

Considering I've been using this router since 2018, I was almost convinced it was finally time to upgrade when I ran into this issue. With all these Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 7 routers available today, it's really hard not to. But all I really needed was a different cable, and I already had a spare in the drawer. For now, my router handles my 500Mbps fiber connection just fine, so until I actually hit its limits, I don't see a reason to replace it. Maybe that'll change when I eventually upgrade to a Gigabit plan.

I finally upgraded from gigabit and realized how much my network was holding me back

Gigabit Ethernet is starting struggling with modern home networks.

item.title: I turned my old Pixel into a remote security camera, and it beat buying another camera
item.itunes:title: I turned my old Pixel into a remote security camera, and it beat buying another camera
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've got a pretty robust security system at home, but it comes with a caveat. The entire security system runs over Power over Ethernet and connects to my Ubiquiti NVR. This makes adding additional security cameras a bit of a headache, so to speak. I can't run PoE everywhere, nor does every room need it. Stepping out for a weekend trip, I wanted to add one more security camera to the mix. So, instead of trying to set up a temporary cable across my home, I decided to use an old Pixel smartphone as a security camera instead.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

There are plenty of apps that claim to enable the feature, but I wanted something tried, tested, and reliable. So, I turned to Alfred Camera. This app gives you remote streaming, motion detection, notifications, and even two-way audio. Basically, all the features you expect from a security system.

Sure, some of the features are locked behind a paywall, but it's turned out to be a surprisingly practical way to reuse an old smartphone as a security camera, and I can see myself using this more than I expected.

I turned my old webcam into a security camera for my home office — here's how you can do it too

Repurpose your old webcam as a surveillance tool

1
By  Sumukh Rao

Setting up Alfred Camera takes minutes at most

Turn any smartphone into a remotely accessible security camera

Alfred Camera is a very simple app in concept, and needs two devices to work effectively. Just install the app on two smartphones, designate one as the camera and the other as a viewer. I installed it on my Pixel and paired my current smartphone as a viewer using a QR code. However, if you choose, you can even use a web browser as a viewer.

The entire process is extremely simple and doesn't require you to mess around with network configurations, opening ports, or setting up a device on your home network. Alfred Camera handles the remote connection and lets you stream the camera feed from your designated camera device anywhere in the world.

In my case, since I was only looking at occasional use, the fully integrated app and viewer ecosystem means I don't need to integrate the camera into my existing Home Assistant-based smart home. Sure, the footage won't be going to my UniFi NVR, but for one-off use, that doesn't really matter.

As far as usage goes, the biggest thing you'll need to worry about is positioning your smartphone. Since I was primarily interested in monitoring activity inside my home while I was away, I placed it on a table with a clear view of the rest of my study. It goes without saying that I also connected it to a charger so that the phone won't burn through its battery in just a few hours.

With the basic setup done, that's basically it. I could log in from my phone and laptop and view the stream practically immediately.

Alfred Camera has plenty of features up its sleeve

From two-way audio to low-light enhancements and motion detection

While the base feature is pretty amazing on its own, Alfred Camera offers a lot more under the hood to bring the experience as close to a proper security camera as possible. For example, you'll find two-way audio support. While for my use case, I've never really needed this, the feature lets you use the microphone and speaker on the Pixel or any other smartphone to communicate with someone at the other end. If you so choose, you can even use it to listen to ambient in-room audio at the camera end.

Another handy addition is the low-light filter. Your smartphone obviously doesn't have infrared lights built in to illuminate dark corners of the room, so software processing is the next best step.

Alfred Camera uses processing to bring out more contrast in an image, making it just a bit easier to view darkened rooms.

All that said, being able to view a camera feed is certainly useful, but I don't want to keep an app open all the time to check what's happening. To solve that problem, Alfred Camera includes motion detection support.

The app can detect changes in movement in front of the camera as part of its monitoring and can shoot across an alert anytime that happens. It also captures a quick event clip anytime it does that, exactly like a proper security camera.

As I mentioned, some of the features are locked behind a subscription paywall. That includes high-resolution live streams, longer-duration recording, as well as smart detections. While the free plan includes basic motion detection, smart detections can tell you exactly what it detected, be it a pet, a person, a vehicle, or even ambient sound level.

If you plan to use this setup with any frequency, you might want to look into the premium tier because those smart alerts mean the difference between being alerted to something as basic as the light shifting in your room and getting alerted only when something deserves your attention.

All that said, there's one more difference between the free and premium versions worth keeping in mind. While the free version of the app stores all footage directly on the phone, the premium plan offloads camera footage in eight-hour blocks to the cloud, making it much easier to review the footage.

A handy way to add temporary security without buying fresh hardware

Like I mentioned when I started off this article, my home already has a comprehensive security setup. That also means that adding additional cameras is a bigger chore than it needs to be. For one-off use, Alfred Camera allows me to turn one of the many phones I have lying around into a proper security camera. I get live streaming, motion alerts, and two-way audio without having to buy another piece of hardware.

It's not something you should be using for 24/7 monitoring because phones aren't meant for it, but if you need a bit of extra security in a part of your home or office, this setup handily serves in a pinch.

AlfredCamera

The AlfredCamera app allows you to repurpose your smartphone as a security camera, or monitor your webcam's feed from your computer remotely.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you're someone who loves gaming, you know that hardware matters. Sure, you can have tons of skill, but the equipment you use can give you an edge for sure. And there are many different parts to make this all come together, but a mouse is an essential piece that you should never skip. While there are many options, the Razer DeathAdder V3 Pro is going to be a top choice, especially now that it can be had for 47% off from Amazon, knocking it down to $80 for a limited time.

The Razer DeathAdder V3 Pro is about as good as you can get for a gaming mouse. It has Razer's impressive Focus Pro 30K optical sensor, optical mouse switches, up to 90 hours of battery life, and is relatively large without weighing too much. It's an absolute joy to use.

See at Amazon

This works even if you don't game

While it might sound strange to buy a gaming mouse for regular use, it actually makes sense. Not only do you get top of the line hardware, but you also get customization options that you'd never find on a basic mouse.

With the Razer DeathAdder V3 Pro, you can adjust the DPI, changing how responsive the mouse will be. It also has buttons that can be customized. Some would even argue that gaming mice have better construction, which means prolonged life do to enhanced durability.

The DeathAdder V3 Pro has a comfortable design and weighs in at just 63 grams. It also features a Razer Focus Pro 30K optical sensor that can track on virtually any surface, even glass.

In addition, this mouse brings an "improved 90-million click life cycle with zero double-clicking issues, to a blistering 0.2ms actuation with no debounce delay." You also get an impressive wireless connection with up to 90 hours of battery life.

It's an easy one to recommend, especially at its newly discounted price.

Silicon lottery dictates the default BIOS settings

It's because of this “silicon lottery,” the natural variance in silicon quality, binning, and grading during manufacturing, that chips from the exact same wafer can have large variance in their power requirements. However, we don't know what kind of silicon we are getting until we boot it up, run some workloads, and test it. Take a flagship CPU like the infamous power-hungry Core i9 14900K, for example. In one instance, one sample of a 14900K might clock exceptionally well and easily hit 6 GHz under favorable circumstances; we call that a golden sample, but on that same motherboard, if you drop in a different 14900K, it might refuse to stay stable even at 5.9 GHz on all cores, with stock voltage and even with the E-cores shut off.

The point is, the motherboard doesn’t know whether you have a golden sample or a dud; it recognizes the 14900K through the CPU’s register, then blasts both chips with maximum voltage just to be safe, and we all know how that went.

Applying a negative offset helps stabilize power, thermals, and more

Based on my tests across recent motherboard BIOS updates, the newer microcodes released to fix that oxidation problem have largely locked down the ability to apply a simple undervolt. Features like Current Excursion Protection (CEP) intentionally throttle performance if they detect the voltage dropping below the hardcoded factory curve.

But there has always been a way: downgrading the BIOS so you can use the older 0x104 microcode properly and pull off a smooth negative offset without CEP. There is risk involved, but the thermal results can be pretty impressive. However, I have seen quite a few newly released or revised LGA 1700 motherboards, even premium Z-series boards, that no longer let you manually select a microcode version. On those locked-down boards, you're stuck tweaking only the basic offset values and hoping for the best.

With that out of the way, here’s how I tested my processor’s behavior and monitored how my motherboard handled power delivery. On a side note, AMD (AM4/AM5) systems follow this exact concept too, though undervolting is much simpler thanks to tech like Precision Boost Overdrive (PBO) and the Curve Optimizer.

A small tweak breathed new life into my CPU

By  Ty Sherback

Establishing the baseline, the crash point, and the sweet spot

Testing voltage limits safely to eliminate thermal throttling

Starting with my test setup, which comprises an Intel Core i5 13600K and an MSI B760M-A-DDR5 motherboard, my motherboard’s VRM isn't super fancy, and my CPU doesn't require much more. However, in stock settings, I did see thermal throttling during shader compilation or while playing games like Borderlands 4, which are incredibly CPU-demanding. To be fair, my CPU cooler isn't fancy either; it's a DeepCool AG300, and given its cooling capacity (165W), pairing it with a 13600K is ambitious, but that isn't the point.

What I observed in this setup while playing games is that the CPU draws voltage close to 1.325V while maintaining 5.1 GHz. My other setup also has a 13600K paired with an ASUS ROG Z790E-Gaming, and there, in stock, that CPU reported 1.350 V.

That's what threw me off. I bought a pair of 13600Ks because I knew how efficient they were, clock for clock, and both the Vcore results are something an average 14900K would use to hit 5.7-5.8 GHz all-core. But what's the point in pushing this much voltage for just 5.1 GHz? I thought my silicon was that bad, but the two CPUs did actually give me some ground to experiment with.

Before I put in any numbers, there is a slight catch when tuning CPU voltage on motherboards that aren't Z-series. From my experience, B-series boards, like mine, operate dynamically and don't let you set a fixed voltage for the P-cores directly. That is why I had to opt for the No(UVP) or the 0x104 microcode and start with a -150 mV undervolt, which translates to 1.000V on the VID Vcore under automatic LLC settings. We can, however, set the voltage directly and even toggle CEP on Z790 boards.

At 1.000V on the B760, with VID (Vcore) at 5.1 GHz, it instantly crashed on boot; then I bumped it to 1.050V, which booted but hard-locked in Windows. Then, I settled on 1,100 V, which booted fine but hard-locked during the Cinebench R23 stability test as well as OCCT. After that, I went to 1.150 volts, which ran through R23 and OCCT but crashed in certain games like Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2, though it ran Borderlands 4 and other titles that rely heavily on multi-core usage.

I won't get into super details here, but from my experience, I knew the automatic Load Line Calibration (LLC) was a factor and was causing crashes. Since my B760 motherboard doesn't have such a fancy VRM, the LLC settings make little sense beyond the 8 stages it provides. After a lot of trial and error, I managed to get the Vcore at a sweet spot of 1.250 volts at the stock 5.1 GHz; for LLC, I set it to stage 3, and guess what: the AG300 cooler handled the heat just fine. The temps don't cross 85 degrees, even with R23/OCCT running. No more thermal throttling whatsoever, given any workload. For gaming and other work, whatever I run, the CPU clocks stay pinned at 5.1 GHz, and thanks to the lower voltage, the motherboard's VRM also doesn't limit the CPU's clock speeds.

MSI motherboards do this exact thing, which I did, and have a feature called CPU Lite Load. I haven't used that here because the implementation differs across boards, mainly due to the VRM and how they respond to LLC stages.

Doesn’t intentionally crashing your PC cause permanent hardware damage?

The actual risk of your system getting damaged is pretty low

Tweaking BIOS power settings, undervolting, and playing with Load Line Calibration isn’t something you do every day unless you do it for a living. As for hardware damage, undervolting, in particular, cannot damage your hardware directly; if the voltage drops too low, the motherboard simply fails to power the chip, causing your PC to shut down abruptly. If you have an NVMe SSD as a boot drive, then with that sudden halt, do not worry.

There is a very, very rare possibility, though I haven't encountered it yet, that the halt permanently corrupts your Windows installation or even takes down the SSD. The worst you can face, as it happened to me a couple of times, is a corrupted Windows boot manager, which is an easy fix via the bcdedit command.

Taking control of your hardware is always worth the effort

Finding your processor’s voltage saves you from the mercy of the auto settings

My testing showed that the Core i5-13600K could maintain its expected clock speeds at a lower operating voltage, reducing temperatures enough to avoid the thermal throttling I had previously encountered. However, finding stable settings required repeated testing, and the results are specific to my processor, motherboard, and cooling setup.

Undervolting can be a useful way to improve efficiency, but it isn't a guaranteed performance upgrade or a fix for degraded hardware. For most users, keeping the BIOS updated, using manufacturer-recommended settings, and ensuring adequate cooling should come first. Voltage tuning is worth exploring when there's a measurable problem to solve and enough time to test the results properly.

item.title: I turned my car's Android Auto screen into a radio with 45,000 stations, and it didn't cost a dime
item.itunes:title: I turned my car's Android Auto screen into a radio with 45,000 stations, and it didn't cost a dime
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I use Android Auto almost every time I get into my car, but most of the time, I'm either listening to music on Spotify or following directions on Google Maps. I rarely bother with the radio anymore, partly because there's only so much you can find on local FM stations. However, I recently came across an app that made me interested in radio again. It brings more than 45,000 internet radio stations from around the world to Android Auto, and you can browse and play them directly from your car's infotainment screen. The best part is that it's completely free, requires no subscription, and works with Android Auto without any complicated setup.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

RadioShake brings thousands of stations to Android Auto

There's a lot more to explore beyond FM

The app I'm talking about is RadioShake, a free internet radio player for Android that also works with Android Auto. It uses the open Radio Browser directory, which has more than 45,000 stations from around the world. You can browse stations by country, genre, or popularity, so there's a lot more to explore than what you'd normally find on your car's FM radio.

For example, you can tune into a jazz station from Japan, listen to a rock station from the US, or find something broadcasting closer to home. You don't even have to know what you're looking for. You can browse different categories and see what catches your interest. And since these are live radio stations, you never really know what song or program you'll come across next, which is part of what makes radio interesting in the first place.

RadioShake also has a few useful features beyond simply playing stations. It can identify songs playing on supported streams and display the artist, track name, and album artwork. You can save stations to your favorites, access your listening history, and even add custom streams if a particular station isn't listed in the directory.

It also supports podcasts, including offline downloads, although I'm more interested in the live radio functionality. The important thing to understand is that RadioShake streams stations over the internet rather than picking up FM signals, so you'll need a mobile data connection to listen. The app itself is free, with no ads or subscription fees to worry about.

I replaced YouTube Music with a 15-year-old app on Android Auto

Convenience versus control behind the wheel

5
By  Parth Shah

Getting RadioShake running on Android Auto is easy

No sideloading or complicated setup required

One thing I appreciate about RadioShake is that it supports Android Auto natively, so you don't need to sideload an APK or use any third-party tools to get it working. You can download it directly from the Google Play Store, open it on your phone, and connect to Android Auto as you normally would. The app should appear in your Android Auto app drawer alongside Spotify, YouTube Music, and other supported media players.

Once you launch RadioShake on your car's screen, you get a simplified interface designed for Android Auto. Separate sections let you browse stations, access your saved favorites, and listen to podcasts. You can explore stations by genre or country and select one to start streaming. The playback screen displays the station's artwork along with the usual media controls, so you don't have to reach for your phone every time you want to change something.

I'd recommend spending a little time exploring stations on your phone and adding the ones you like to your favorites before getting into the car. That way, you have a collection of stations ready to play without having to browse through thousands of options on the dashboard.

Another useful feature introduced in version 3.9 is automatic playback. You can enable it in the app's settings so RadioShake resumes your last station whenever the app launches. It's disabled by default, but it's worth enabling if you want the radio to start playing without having to select a station every time you get into your car.

RadioShake makes listening to the radio fun again

Sometimes it's better to let someone else pick the music

One thing I've noticed about music streaming apps is I often end up listening to the same songs and playlists. Apps like Spotify are great when I know exactly what I want to hear, but sometimes I spend more time deciding what to play than actually listening to music. RadioShake offers a nice change from that.

There's also something interesting about listening to stations from other countries. You get to discover music that probably wouldn't make it into your usual recommendations, and you can switch between different genres or regions whenever you want. Unlike a playlist, you don't get to skip individual songs, but that's part of the appeal.

Of course, there are a few limitations. Since RadioShake relies on internet streams, the experience depends on your mobile data connection. You might run into buffering when driving through areas with poor coverage, and the audio quality also varies depending on the station. Some stations have their own advertisements, even though RadioShake itself doesn't show any.

A refreshing change from my usual playlists

I don't see RadioShake replacing Spotify or YouTube Music for me, especially when I want to listen to something specific. But it's a refreshing alternative, and having access to so many stations makes it worth keeping on my Android Auto screen.

You can download it directly from the Google Play Store, open it on your phone, and connect to Android Auto as you normally would. The app should appear in your Android Auto app drawer alongside Spotify, YouTube Music, and other supported media players.

Once you launch RadioShake on your car's screen, you get a simplified interface designed for Android Auto. Separate sections let you browse stations, access your saved favorites, and listen to podcasts. You can explore stations by genre or country and select one to start streaming. The playback screen displays the station's artwork along with the usual media controls, so you don't have to reach for your phone every time you want to change something.

I'd recommend spending a little time exploring stations on your phone and adding the ones you like to your favorites before getting into the car. That way, you have a collection of stations ready to play without having to browse through thousands of options on the dashboard.

Another useful feature introduced in version 3.9 is automatic playback. You can enable it in the app's settings so RadioShake resumes your last station whenever the app launches. It's disabled by default, but it's worth enabling if you want the radio to start playing without having to select a station every time you get into your car.

Sometimes it's better to let someone else pick the music

One thing I've noticed about music streaming apps is I often end up listening to the same songs and playlists. Apps like Spotify are great when I know exactly what I want to hear, but sometimes I spend more time deciding what to play than actually listening to music. RadioShake offers a nice change from that.

There's also something interesting about listening to stations from other countries. You get to discover music that probably wouldn't make it into your usual recommendations, and you can switch between different genres or regions whenever you want. Unlike a playlist, you don't get to skip individual songs, but that's part of the appeal.

Of course, there are a few limitations. Since RadioShake relies on internet streams, the experience depends on your mobile data connection. You might run into buffering when driving through areas with poor coverage, and the audio quality also varies depending on the station. Some stations have their own advertisements, even though RadioShake itself doesn't show any.

A refreshing change from my usual playlists

I don't see RadioShake replacing Spotify or YouTube Music for me, especially when I want to listen to something specific. But it's a refreshing alternative, and having access to so many stations makes it worth keeping on my Android Auto screen.

item.title: Windows 11 has enabled Memory Integrity, but gamers shouldn’t worry that much
item.itunes:title: Windows 11 has enabled Memory Integrity, but gamers shouldn’t worry that much
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Microsoft will enable HVCI (memory integrity) on eligible Windows 11 PCs via a recent update.
  • On modern hardware, HVCI causes only modest gaming slowdowns — not the big hit seen on older systems.
  • You can disable HVCI if desired; follow the Windows 11 memory integrity guide to turn it off.

For a little while now, Microsoft has advertised that it would force-enable a feature called Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI) on Windows 11 PCs with the proper hardware to run it.

At the time, it sounded like a potential problem for gamers, as HVCI (also known as 'memory integrity') can make a measurable impact on performance. However, if you're on modern hardware, there's a good chance you won't need to worry at all

Windows 11's HVCI isn't the performance-hungry feature we featured it would be

The effects are pretty modest

Microsoft has pushed the November 10 (KB5132061) update to Windows 11 PCs everywhere. The update pushes everything from the October 28 (KB5127936) Preview update to the Release branch, which includes the following patch note:

New! This update expands memory integrity protection across eligible devices. Supported PCs may now have memory integrity (HVCI) enabled during updates to help improve security and prepare devices for advanced Windows security features, while respecting existing user or IT administrator choices.

When this feature first rolled out a few years ago, it had a pretty measurable effect on gaming performance. However, it seems that with modern hardware, the effects are far less than what we first saw.

We tested memory Integrity's effect on gaming performance a month ago, and the results were very modest. The biggest difference was when we played Cyberpunk 2077 on a newer PC, where we saw it reach 116.8 FPS as its 1% low instead of 124.5 with memory integrity off. Sure, it's an impact, but it's not exactly a catastrophic one.

Still, if you'd rather not have HVCI running at all, you can get rid of it. Check out our guide on how to disable HVCI on Windows 11 for all the instructions and details.

It's not you, Penguin, it's the industry around you
